question.explain: Starlette's Router holds an ordered list of routes and is asked, for each incoming request, to pick exactly one to handle it. The Match enum (NONE/PARTIAL/FULL) is how each route reports whether and how well it fits.
question.question: How does a Starlette Router decide which route handles an incoming request when several routes are registered?
question.reference_answer: Router.app iterates self.routes in registration order, calling route.matches(scope) on each. The first route that returns Match.FULL updates the scope, has its handle() called, and iteration stops. A Match.PARTIAL (path matches but method does not) is only recorded — the first one seen — and used as a fallback if the whole list produces no FULL match, which is how 405 Method Not Allowed is produced. If nothing matches, redirect_slashes may retry, otherwise the default handler returns 404.

rubric.text: Routes are checked in the order they were registered.
The first route that returns a full match handles the request and the search stops.
A partial match (path matches, method does not) is only used when no full match is found.
A request that matches no route falls through to a 404 via the default handler.

anti_criteria.text: Routes are ranked by path specificity or longest matching prefix.
The router collects every matching route and then picks the best one.

question.transfer_problem: If two Route objects have overlapping paths, which one wins, and why?

items.answer: The router walks its list of routes in the order you registered them and calls .matches() on each. The first one that comes back as a full match gets to handle the request and it stops looking. If a route's path matches but the HTTP method doesn't, that's a partial match — it hangs onto that and only uses it if no route fully matches, which is how you get a 405. If nothing matches at all it falls through to the default 404 handler.

question.explain: A Starlette Response can carry a background task. Both the timing of that task relative to the response bytes and the ordering of multiple tasks are fixed by the framework, not by the caller.
question.question: When does a Starlette response run its attached background task, and in what order do multiple tasks run?
question.reference_answer: Response.__call__ sends the response start and body first, and only then, if self.background is not None, awaits it — so the client receives the full response before the task runs. BackgroundTasks.__call__ iterates its task list and awaits each task in sequence, so tasks run one after another in the order they were added, not concurrently. A sync task function is run in a threadpool via run_in_threadpool; an async one is awaited directly.

rubric.text: The background task runs after the response body has been sent to the client.
BackgroundTasks awaits its tasks one at a time, in the order they were added.
A synchronous task function is executed in a threadpool.
The task is only awaited when response.background is not None.

anti_criteria.text: The background task runs before, or concurrently with, sending the response.
Multiple background tasks are run concurrently or in parallel.

question.transfer_problem: If one background task raises, do the remaining tasks still run?

items.answer: The response is sent first — headers and body go out to the client — and then Response.__call__ awaits self.background if one was set. So the client isn't kept waiting for the task. If you use BackgroundTasks with several tasks, they run in a loop, awaited one at a time in the order you added them, so it's sequential not parallel. Sync functions get pushed to a threadpool so they don't block the event loop.

question.explain: Starlette splits exception handling across two middlewares at opposite ends of the stack. Knowing which one does what explains why some errors become clean 4xx responses and others become 500s.
question.question: What is the difference in responsibility between ExceptionMiddleware and ServerErrorMiddleware in Starlette's middleware stack?
question.reference_answer: ServerErrorMiddleware is the outermost middleware: it catches any otherwise-unhandled exception, returns a 500 (or a debug traceback), and then always re-raises so the server can log it. ExceptionMiddleware is installed innermost, just outside the router: it maps expected exceptions — HTTPException and WebSocketException, plus handlers you register by class or status code — to responses, and does not re-raise. Because ExceptionMiddleware sits inside user middleware, it does not catch exceptions raised by user middleware; those reach ServerErrorMiddleware as 500s.

rubric.text: ServerErrorMiddleware is the outermost middleware and turns otherwise-unhandled errors into 500s.
ServerErrorMiddleware re-raises the exception after sending its response.
ExceptionMiddleware maps HTTPException and registered handlers to responses without re-raising.
ExceptionMiddleware is installed innermost, closest to the router.
Because ExceptionMiddleware is inside user middleware, it does not catch errors raised by user middleware.

anti_criteria.text: ExceptionMiddleware is the outermost middleware and the first to see a request.
ServerErrorMiddleware swallows the exception and does not propagate it.

question.transfer_problem: An HTTPException(404) is raised by a plain-ASGI middleware you added. What status does the client see, and which middleware produced it?

items.answer: ServerErrorMiddleware wraps everything — it's the outermost layer. Anything that isn't handled deeper down bubbles up to it, it returns a 500 (or the debug traceback page), and crucially it re-raises the exception afterwards so your server logs still see it. ExceptionMiddleware is right next to the router, the innermost middleware. Its job is to turn HTTPException and any handlers you registered into normal responses, and it doesn't re-raise. One consequence: since it's inside your own middleware, an exception thrown by your middleware won't be caught by it and ends up as a 500 from ServerErrorMiddleware.

question.explain: The Match enum has NONE=0, PARTIAL=1, FULL=2. It is tempting to read those integers as a global priority the router sorts on. This question is about how Router.app actually uses PARTIAL vs FULL.
question.question: The Match enum has values NONE=0, PARTIAL=1, FULL=2. How does Router.app use the distinction between PARTIAL and FULL when several routes could respond?
question.reference_answer: Router.app loops routes in order. The moment a route returns Match.FULL it updates the scope, calls that route's handle(), and returns — no later route is consulted. A Match.PARTIAL result is only stashed (the first one seen) in the partial variable; the router keeps looking for a FULL match. Only after the loop finds no FULL match does it fall back to the stashed partial and call its handle(), which is what lets a path-but-not-method match produce a 405 rather than a 404. NONE contributes nothing.

rubric.text: A FULL match is acted on immediately and ends the route search.
A PARTIAL match is only used as a fallback after the whole list yields no FULL match.
Only the first PARTIAL match encountered is kept.
The PARTIAL fallback is what produces 405 Method Not Allowed instead of 404.

anti_criteria.text: The router compares the numeric Match values of all routes and dispatches to the highest.
A PARTIAL match short-circuits the route search the same way a FULL match does.

question.transfer_problem: Two routes both return PARTIAL for a request. Which one handles it?

items.answer: The loop goes route by route. If a route says FULL, the router immediately updates the scope and calls that route's handle and returns — it never looks at routes further down the list. If a route says PARTIAL, the router just records it (only the first PARTIAL it sees) and carries on looking for a FULL match. If it gets to the end with no FULL match, then it uses that recorded partial route, and that's the mechanism that gives you a 405 for a known path with the wrong method.

question.explain: An endpoint function is invoked from Route.handle, yet an HTTPException it raises still comes back as a proper HTTP response. This question is about the wrapper that makes that happen and where it lives.
question.question: How does an HTTPException raised inside an endpoint function get turned into an HTTP response, given that the endpoint is invoked from Route.handle?
question.reference_answer: request_response wraps the endpoint call in wrap_app_handling_exceptions before invoking it (Route.handle just calls self.app). When the endpoint raises, that wrapper catches it; for an HTTPException it first looks for a handler registered against the exact status code, then walks the exception's MRO for a class-based handler. ExceptionMiddleware seeded the default HTTPException handler, so the lookup finds http_exception, which returns a PlainTextResponse with the exception's detail and status code. If the wrapper finds no handler it re-raises; if the response had already started it raises a RuntimeError instead.

rubric.text: The endpoint invocation is wrapped by wrap_app_handling_exceptions.
For an HTTPException the wrapper checks a status-code handler before a class-based handler.
The class-based handler lookup walks the exception type's MRO.
If no handler is found the exception is re-raised.
If the response has already started, a RuntimeError is raised instead of handling.

anti_criteria.text: Route.handle itself contains the try/except that converts the exception.
The exception propagates to ServerErrorMiddleware, which renders the HTTPException as its response.

question.transfer_problem: You register a handler for the base class Exception but not for HTTPException. Does an HTTPException hit your handler?

items.answer: Route.handle just calls self.app, and for a function endpoint self.app is what request_response built — which wraps the actual call to your endpoint in wrap_app_handling_exceptions. So when your endpoint raises HTTPException, that wrapper is the thing that catches it. For an HTTPException it looks up a handler by the exact status code first, and if there isn't one it walks the exception class's MRO looking for a class handler. The default HTTPException handler that ExceptionMiddleware registered turns it into a PlainTextResponse. If no handler matches at all, the wrapper just re-raises.
